passages.text: <italic toggle="yes">Ex situ</italic> generation of stoichiometric HCN and its application in the Pd-catalysed cyanation of aryl bromides: evidence for a transmetallation step between two oxidative addition Pd-complexes† †Electronic supplementary information (ESI) available. <sentence_start/>CCDC 1504904-1504908. <sentence_start/>For ESI and crystallographic data in CIF or other electronic format see DOI: 10.1039/c7sc03912c
We demonstrate how hydrogen cyanide can be exploited for the cyanation of aryl bromides with Pd-catalysis.

A protocol for the Pd-catalysed cyanation of aryl bromides using near stoichiometric and gaseous hydrogen cyanide is reported for the first time. <sentence_start/>A two-chamber reactor was adopted for the safe liberation of <italic toggle="yes">ex situ</italic> generated HCN in a closed environment, which proved highly efficient in the Ni-catalysed hydrocyanation as the test reaction. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, this setup was exploited for converting a range of aryl and heteroaryl bromides (28 examples) directly into the corresponding benzonitriles in high yields, without the need for cyanide salts. <sentence_start/>Cyanation was achieved employing the Pd(0) precatalyst, P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>-Pd-G3 and a weak base, potassium acetate, in a dioxane-water solvent mixture. <sentence_start/>The methodology was also suitable for the synthesis of <sup>13</sup>C-labelled benzonitriles with <italic toggle="yes">ex situ</italic> generated <sup>13</sup>C-hydrogen cyanide. <sentence_start/>Stoichiometric studies with the metal complexes were undertaken to delineate the mechanism for this catalytic transformation. <sentence_start/>Treatment of Pd(P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> with H<sup>13</sup>CN in THF provided two Pd-hydride complexes, (P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Pd(H)(<sup>13</sup>CN), and [(P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>)Pd(H)]<sub>2</sub>Pd(<sup>13</sup>CN)<sub>4</sub>, both of which were isolated and characterised by NMR spectroscopy and X-ray crystal structure analysis. <sentence_start/>When the same reaction was performed in a THF : water mixture in the presence of KOAc, only (P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Pd(H)(<sup>13</sup>CN) was formed. <sentence_start/>Subjection of this cyano hydride metal complex with the oxidative addition complex (P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>)Pd(Ph)(Br) in a 1 : 1 ratio in THF led to a transmetallation step with the formation of (P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Pd(H)(Br) and <sup>13</sup>C-benzonitrile from a reductive elimination step. <sentence_start/>These experiments suggest the possibility of a catalytic cycle involving initially the formation of two Pd(<sc>ii</sc>)-species from the oxidative addition of L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(0) into HCN and an aryl bromide followed by a transmetallation step to L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(Ar)(CN) and L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(H)(Br), which both reductively eliminate, the latter in the presence of KOAc, to generate the benzonitrile and L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(0).
Introduction

Benzonitriles are a valuable class of compounds with a broad range of applications serving as important substructures in many agrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, dyes, polymers and other organic materials.<citation rid="cit1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11456474" doi="10.1021/ar0000354" count="1">1</citation> <sentence_start/>The nitrile group is also a precursor to a variety of important functionalities such as aldehydes, ketones, carboxamides and carboxylates.<citation rid="cit2" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2</citation> <sentence_start/>Conventional means for the instalment of a cyanide group onto an aromatic ring include the Rosenmund-von Braun or Sandmeyer reactions applying stoichiometric CuCN with aryl halides or diazonium salts.<citation rid="cit3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20291034" doi="10.1021/cr60126a003" count="1">3</citation> <sentence_start/>Yet, in the last decade, transition metal catalysed cyanations of aromatic halides with metal complexes based on copper,<citation rid="cit4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17480048" doi="10.1002/chem.200700079" count="1">4</citation> nickel<citation rid="cit5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28379009" doi="10.1021/acs.orglett.7b00732" count="1">5</citation> and palladium<citation rid="cit6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12698441" doi="10.1002/chem.200390210" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="cit7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21528150" doi="10.1039/c1cs15004a" count="1">7</citation> have held a key position. <sentence_start/>In particular, the protocols based on Pd-catalysis through the extensive work by Beller,<citation rid="cit7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21528150" doi="10.1039/c1cs15004a" count="1">7</citation> Grushin<citation rid="cit8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21699208" doi="10.1021/ja2042035" count="1">8</citation> and Buchwald<citation rid="cit9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/ol5032359" pmcid="PMC4301087" pmid="25555140" count="1">9</citation> are characterised by relatively mild reaction conditions and good functional group tolerance. <sentence_start/>A variety of different cyanide sources have been applied including salts or derivatives such as NaCN,<citation rid="cit8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21699208" doi="10.1021/ja2042035" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="cit10" ref-type="bibr" count="1">10</citation> KCN,<citation rid="cit6a" ref-type="bibr" count="1">6a</citation>,<citation rid="cit6c" ref-type="bibr" count="1">c</citation>,<citation rid="cit6d" ref-type="bibr" count="1">d</citation>,<citation rid="cit11" ref-type="bibr" count="1">11</citation> (Me)<sub>3</sub>SiCN,<citation rid="cit12" ref-type="bibr" count="1">12</citation> acetone cyanohydrin,<citation rid="cit13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/anie.200250778" pmid="12698471" count="1">13</citation> K<sub>4</sub>Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>,<citation rid="cit9a" ref-type="bibr" count="1">9a</citation>,<citation rid="cit14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/chem.200700079" pmid="17480048" count="1">14</citation> Zn(CN)<sub>2</sub>,<citation rid="cit9b" ref-type="bibr" count="1">9b</citation>,<citation rid="cit15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11073607" doi="10.1021/jo0009954" count="1">15</citation> CuCN,<citation rid="cit16" ref-type="bibr" count="1">16</citation><italic toggle="yes">etc.</italic> (Scheme 1). <sentence_start/>However, many of these sources also have their disadvantages. <sentence_start/>For example, metal contaminants can become an issue with the use of potassium ferrocyanide, whereas with the cyanohydrin of acetone, this chemical must be stored carefully and is approx. 20 times more costly than potassium cyanide.‡
‡According to the Sigma-Aldrich catalogue, 5 g of acetone cyanohydrin costs the same as approximately 100 g of potassium cyanide.

Furthermore, considering the fact that all of these cyanide precursors originate from hydrogen cyanide (HCN), which is produced on a million-ton scale size <italic toggle="yes">via</italic> the Andrussow<citation rid="cit17" ref-type="bibr" count="1">17</citation> and BMA-Degussa processes<citation rid="cit18" ref-type="bibr" count="1">18</citation> from natural gas and ammonia or as a byproduct in acrylonitrile production,<citation rid="cit18" ref-type="bibr" count="1">18</citation>,<citation rid="cit19" ref-type="bibr" count="1">19</citation> there could be an interest in the development of a cyanation process of aryl halides exploiting this original source of cyanide, namely gaseous HCN.<citation rid="cit20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27595239" doi="10.1002/chem.201604061" count="1">20</citation>
Scheme 1
Previous developments in Pd-catalysed cyanation protocols and our new approach applying gaseous HCN.

Only three reports are found in the literature applying HCN directly or by its <italic toggle="yes">in situ</italic> formation. <sentence_start/>In 2015, Buchwald and Hooker reported a <sup>11</sup>C-cyanation study for the synthesis of aromatic cyanides with applications for positron emission tomography (PET).<citation rid="cit21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25565277" doi="10.1021/ja512115s" pmcid="PMC4394387" count="1">21</citation> <sentence_start/>Here, submicromolar amounts of gaseous H<sup>11</sup>CN dissolved in THF were introduced to a 1000-fold excess of preformed oxidative addition palladium(<sc>ii</sc>) complex, affording the desired <sup>11</sup>C-benzonitriles nearly instantaneously. <sentence_start/>A follow-up paper by the same two groups demonstrated the possibilities of this approach for the <sup>11</sup>C-labelling of unprotected peptides.<citation rid="cit22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28502164" doi="10.1021/jacs.7b02761" pmcid="PMC5572217" count="1">22</citation> <sentence_start/>Alternatively, Beller and co-workers reported the <italic toggle="yes">in situ</italic> release of HCN from acetone cyanohydrin although this was carried out in the presence of sodium carbonate, which undoubtedly leads to the direct formation of the reactive cyanide anion species.<citation rid="cit13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/anie.200250778" pmid="12698471" count="1">13</citation>

Nevertheless, there is a reluctance to apply HCN (b.p. 27 °C) as a cyanation reagent in an academic setting or an R&D laboratory, which is undoubtedly linked to the high toxicity and explosive nature of this gaseous one-carbon reagent, thereby complicating its handling, storage and transportation.<citation rid="cit23" ref-type="bibr" count="1">23</citation> <sentence_start/>Another challenge in the use of hydrogen cyanide as a cyanation reagent is how to control its dosage in stoichiometric amounts as Pd-catalysed cyanations of aryl halides are particularly sensitive to the cyanide concentrations. <sentence_start/>The strong binding of cyanide anion to transition metals can lead to catalyst deactivation if present in elevated concentrations.<citation rid="cit7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21528150" doi="10.1039/c1cs15004a" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="cit24" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25493420" doi="10.1021/cr5004375" count="1">24</citation> <sentence_start/>With other cyanide reagents, this complication is normally addressed by their slow addition to the reaction mixture, slow mass transport of the cyanide anion by specific water/organic solvents mixtures or by use of cyanide complexes with low solubilities.<citation rid="cit8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21699208" doi="10.1021/ja2042035" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="cit9b" ref-type="bibr" count="1">9b</citation>,<citation rid="cit13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/anie.200250778" pmid="12698471" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="cit14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/chem.200700079" pmid="17480048" count="1">14</citation> <sentence_start/>Grushin and co-workers have published impressive and detailed studies on the mechanism of cyanide induced catalyst deactivation in the Pd-catalysed cyanation of aromatic halides. <sentence_start/>In their work, they report that addition of an excess of <sup>13</sup>C-labelled potassium cyanide (K<sup>13</sup>CN) to different intermediates of the catalytic cycle in the Pd-catalysed cyanation of iodobenzene led to coordinatively saturated and catalytically inactive palladium complexes such as [Pd(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>, [HPd(CN)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> or [ArPd(CN)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>.<citation rid="cit25" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17199273" doi="10.1021/ja066931d" count="1">25</citation> <sentence_start/>More interestingly, the same group revealed that traces of water in the reaction mixture combined with K<sup>13</sup>CN forms H<sup>13</sup>CN that immediately undergoes oxidative addition with Pd(0) leading to the same coordinatively saturated and off-cycle palladium complexes with concurrent formation of hydrogen gas.<citation rid="cit26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18336024" doi="10.1021/ja078298h" count="1">26</citation>

In this paper, we report on the direct use of industrially important hydrogen cyanide in the palladium-catalysed cyanation of (hetero)aromatic bromides (Scheme 1). <sentence_start/>These results deviate from conventional wisdom, since Grushin's earlier work demonstrated the propensity of palladium(0) to undergo fast oxidative addition into the H-CN bond shutting down the catalytic cycle. <sentence_start/>And yet, our results demonstrate that conditions can be identified whereby the presence of HCN does not terminate the cyanation reaction, but enhances the reactivity vis-à-vis cyanide salts. <sentence_start/>Secondly and most important, we describe a simple and safe setup whereby HCN is delivered in stoichiometric amounts by <italic toggle="yes">ex situ</italic> generation in a two-chamber reactor, thereby providing a simple and safe setting for handling gaseous HCN in small-scale reactions. <sentence_start/>We demonstrate the usefulness of this setup not only for the Pd-catalysed cyanation of aryl bromides, but also for the Ni-mediated hydrocyanation of styrenes as a test reaction. <sentence_start/>With respect to the cyanation reactions good functional group tolerance was obtained, and the method proved amenable to scale-up, but also to carbon-13 isotope labelling applying H<sup>13</sup>CN. <sentence_start/>Surprisingly, the developed conditions proved to be dependent on water as the co-solvent and the presence of a weak base, KOAc. <sentence_start/>In their absence, catalytic shutdown was observed, thereby indicating the operation of an alternative mechanism to Pd-catalysed cyanations applying cyanide salts. <sentence_start/>Studies and isolation of the oxidative addition complexes suggest a mechanism involving the transmetallation between two palladium(<sc>ii</sc>) species, both formed by the oxidative addition of palladium(0) into either HCN or the aryl bromide electrophile.
Results and discussion
Hydrogen cyanide releasing studies

In order to provide a system for the controlled dosage of hydrogen cyanide in stoichiometric quantities, we envisioned that the two-chamber system previously utilised for the <italic toggle="yes">ex situ</italic> liberation of carbon monoxide,<citation rid="cit27" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26999377" doi="10.1021/acs.accounts.5b00471" count="1">27</citation> hydrogen<citation rid="cit28" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24870212" doi="10.1021/jo500801t" count="1">28</citation> and ethylene<citation rid="cit29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24243666" doi="10.1002/chem.201303668" count="1">29</citation> from specific nongaseous precursors could be exploited. <sentence_start/>Such an approach would provide a simple and safe setup without the direct handling of HCN gas. <sentence_start/>Hence, our focus was first directed to identifying a suitable system for the generation of HCN gas under a closed environment, and the well-established nickel-catalysed hydrocyanation of olefins was exploited as a test system for the optimisation.<citation rid="cit30" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19637256" doi="10.1002/chem.200802611" count="1">30</citation>-<citation rid="cit32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/c0cc01452d" pmid="20972491" count="1">32</citation> After considerable experimentation on the hydrocyanation of styrene (see ESI†), we finally adopted the following conditions as illustrated in Scheme 2. <sentence_start/>A combination of KCN, ethylene glycol and AcOH provided the desired release of gaseous HCN. <sentence_start/>Ethylene glycol serves a dual purpose acting both as solvent while simultaneously ensuring separation of the AcOH from KCN until stirring is initiated. <sentence_start/>By utilising this setup for the HCN producing chamber in combination with the Ni-catalysed hydrocyanation conditions in the second chamber (Ni(COD)<sub>2</sub>, XantPhos), a range of different styrenes bearing both electron donating and withdrawing groups could successfully be hydrocyanated to products <bold>1-7</bold> in near quantitative yields. <sentence_start/>Full conversion of all styrene derivatives was attained applying only 1.5 equivalents of KCN for the production of HCN, indicating the effectiveness of this gas generator.
Scheme 2

Ni-catalysed hydrocyanation of styrenes employing a two-chamber system with <italic toggle="yes">ex situ</italic> generated HCN. <sentence_start/><sup>a</sup>Chamber A: styrene (1.0 mmol), Ni(COD)<sub>2</sub> (5.0 mol%), XantPhos (7.5 mol%) and CPME (2 mL). <sentence_start/>Chamber B: KCN (1.5 mmol), ethylene glycol (1 mL), AcOH (9.0 mmol). <sentence_start/>Isolated yields are given as an average of 2 runs.
Studies on the cyanation of (hetero)aryl bromides

With a simple and convenient system for the release of gaseous HCN in hand, we next turned our attention towards the Pd-catalysed cyanation of (hetero)aryl bromides. <sentence_start/>As depicted in the scheme of Table 1, initial optimisation results were carried out with 4-bromoanisole. <sentence_start/>This study revealed that reaction conditions consisting of a catalyst formed from Pd(dba)<sub>2</sub> with P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>, in the presence of hydrogen cyanide (1.5 equiv.), a weak base such as KOAc, and a solvent mixture of water and dioxane could generate 4-methoxybenzonitrile (<bold>8</bold>) with a conversion of 78% according to the <sup>1</sup>H NMR analysis of the crude reaction mixture (Table 1, entry 1). <sentence_start/>P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub> as a ligand proved to be superior to other monodentate and bidentate ligands (entries 2-6; see ESI† section for full optimisation studies), which is in accord with earlier results reported by Grushin and co-workers.<citation rid="cit8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21699208" doi="10.1021/ja2042035" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="cit26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18336024" doi="10.1021/ja078298h" count="1">26</citation> <sentence_start/>In general, weak bases such as KOAc and NaOAc provided better conversions to the desired 4-methoxybenzonitrile, whereas stronger bases including Cy<sub>2</sub>NMe, DBU and Et<sub>3</sub>N all proved inferior (entries 7-9). <sentence_start/>Increasing to three equivalents of KOAc provided a slight increase in the conversion to 82% (entry 10). <sentence_start/>The efficiency of the reaction could also be increased further exploiting the Buchwald pre-catalyst, P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>-Pd-G3, providing a 90% isolated yield of benzonitrile <bold>8</bold> after column chromatography (entry 11). <sentence_start/>Control experiments with omission of either base or palladium precursors resulted in low or no conversion, resp.

Different water : solvent combinations were tested and dioxane proved to be the solvent of choice (entries 12 and 13, see also ESI†). <sentence_start/>Notably, the presence of water as the co-solvent is of key importance as similar experiments applying only dioxane as the solvent resulted in complete catalytic shutdown. <sentence_start/>In our scope studies, we later discovered that a 2 : 1 mixture of water and dioxane provided higher yields for certain substrates, and hence this ratio was used for all subsequent cyanations. <sentence_start/>Not surprisingly and in accord with Grushin's previous results, carrying out the Pd-catalysed cyanation in a single chamber reactor applying KCN directly with or without the addition of acetic acid under the conditions developed led to no formation of <bold>8</bold> (result not shown).

With the optimised reaction conditions in hand, we set out to explore the scope of the Pd-catalysed cyanation using gaseous HCN. <sentence_start/>All yields are reported as an average of two runs and the results are depicted in Scheme 3. <sentence_start/>Aryl bromides carrying electron donating substituents were initially examined. <sentence_start/>Methoxy-, hydroxy-, alkyl- and aryl-substituted aryl bromides provided the desired compounds in high yields ranging from 90% to 97% (compounds <bold>8-11</bold>). <sentence_start/>Electron withdrawing substituents such as cyano, acyl and carboxylate afforded compounds <bold>12</bold>, <bold>13</bold> and <bold>14</bold> in yields attaining quantitative. <sentence_start/>Even <italic toggle="yes">p</italic>-bromobenzoic acid underwent successful coupling affording <italic toggle="yes">p</italic>-cyanobenzoic acid (<bold>15</bold>) in an 86% yield, using 4 equiv. of KOAc combined with 5 mol% of Buchwald's precatalyst. <sentence_start/>The use of phenol and benzoic acid derivatives in the Pd-catalysed cyanation with NaCN were previously shown by Ushkov and Grushin to lead to catalyst deactivation due to the formation of HCN.<citation rid="cit8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21699208" doi="10.1021/ja2042035" count="1">8</citation><italic toggle="yes">p</italic>-Bromobenzaldehyde also proved reactive with the isolation of <bold>16</bold> in a somewhat lower yield. <sentence_start/>This slight reduction in isolated yield can possibly be explained by competing benzoin condensation of both starting material and product. <sentence_start/>The substitution pattern of bromoanilines interfered significantly with the developed conditions and installment of the cyano-functionality onto 2-, 3-, and 4-bromoaniline was achieved in yields of 95%, 77% and 47% respectively (compounds <bold>17-19</bold>). <sentence_start/>Aryl bromides displaying <italic toggle="yes">ortho</italic>-substitutions were also effective for these substitution reactions as illustrated with compounds <bold>17</bold> and <bold>20-22</bold>, all isolated in yields between 92% and 96%. <sentence_start/>However, 2-bromo-1,3-dimethylbenzene did require an increase of the catalyst loading to achieve the high 96% isolated yield of <bold>21</bold>. <sentence_start/>Lowering the reaction temperature of the HCN consuming chamber, from 60 °C to 45 °C, ensured a chemoselective activation of the aromatic bromide in the presence of the <italic toggle="yes">p</italic>-chloride affording <bold>23</bold> in an 88% isolated yield. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, an aryl bromide possessing a benzylic alcohol, and five heteroaromatic bromides were tested under the developed conditions. <sentence_start/>All underwent successful cyanation to afford the desired target molecules in yields ranging from 75% to 95% (compounds <bold>22</bold>, <bold>24-28</bold>). <sentence_start/>It should be mentioned though that despite the successful coupling of these handful of heteroaryl bromides, two other heterocycles tested such as 2-acetyl-5-bromothiophene and 3-bromobenzothiophene failed to provide the corresponding nitrile product. <sentence_start/>The reasons for this catalytic shutdown are not completely understood (see Discussion in next section). <sentence_start/>Finally, attempts to perform catalytic cyanation on 4-biphenyl triflate, applying the developed protocol, were non-rewarding with no conversion observed for this electrophile.
Scheme 3

Pd-catalysed cyanation of aryl bromides. <sentence_start/><sup>a</sup>Chamber A: aryl bromide (1.0 mmol), P(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>Bu)<sub>3</sub>-Pd-G3 (2.5 mol%) and KOAc (3.0 mmol) in dioxane (1 mL) and H<sub>2</sub>O (2 mL). Chamber B: KCN (1.5 mmol) or K<sup>13</sup>CN (1.5 mmol) ethylene glycol (1 mL) and AcOH (9 mmol). <sentence_start/>Isolated yields are given as an average of 2 runs. <sentence_start/><sup>b</sup>5.0 mol% catalyst used. <sentence_start/><sup>c</sup>4.0 equiv. of KOAc used. <sentence_start/><sup>d</sup>HCN consuming chamber only heated to 45 °C.

Next, attention was directed to implementing this developed protocol for <sup>13</sup>C-labelling. <sentence_start/>By simply substituting KCN with its <sup>13</sup>C-labelled counterpart under otherwise unchanged conditions, direct access to isotopically labeled benzonitrile derivatives were achieved. <sentence_start/>Four entries from Scheme 3 were selected for labelling, and all compounds were isolated in near identical yields to the unlabeled compounds (compounds <bold>10-<sup>13</sup>C</bold>, <bold>11-<sup>13</sup>C</bold>, <bold>12-<sup>13</sup>C</bold> and <bold>28-<sup>13</sup>C</bold>).

Finally, the developed protocol was tested for the synthesis of three active pharmaceutical ingredients, namely dapivirine (reverse transcriptase inhibitor), citalopram (serotonin reuptake inhibitor) and letrozole (non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor), the results of which are depicted in Scheme 4.<citation rid="cit33" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20804202" doi="10.1021/jm100762r" pmcid="PMC2988972" count="1">33</citation> <sentence_start/>Dapivirine (<bold>29</bold>) and citalopram (<bold>30</bold>) were obtained in satisfactory 96% and 86% isolated yields, respectively, from the corresponding bromide precursors applying 5.0 mol% of the Buchwald precatalyst. <sentence_start/>For the synthesis of letrozole (<bold>31</bold>) a double cyanation is required with the dibromide <bold>31a</bold>. <sentence_start/>Doubling the loading of KCN for HCN release to 3 equivalents combined with an increase in KOAc to 4 equivalents, gratifyingly afforded the dicyanide <bold>31</bold> in an excellent 97% isolated yield again with 5.0 mol% precatalyst. <sentence_start/>The synthesis of letrozole was then attempted on a fivefold scale combined with a 100 mL two-chamber reactor to afford a near identical isolated yield of 95%. <sentence_start/>Finally, scaling up to 10 mmol in a 200 mL two-chamber reactor, with an HCN release from 30 mmol of KCN, corresponding to more than 700 mL of gaseous HCN, afforded the desired pharmaceutical in a good 85% isolated yield.
Scheme 4
Synthesis of pharmaceuticals by Pd-catalysed cyanation and scale up studies. <sentence_start/><sup>a</sup>For reactions on 1.0 mmol scale, yields are an average of two runs.
Mechanistic investigations

Having established the scope of the Pd-catalysed cyanation of (hetero)aryl bromides with hydrogen cyanide, some questions still remained. <sentence_start/>Given a pKa difference in water for acetic acid (4.76) and HCN (9.21) of almost 4.5 units, indicates that HCN is potentially the reactive species in solution and not the free cyanide anion. <sentence_start/>However, previous reports by Grushin and co-workers clearly demonstrated that the presence of free HCN formed from the protonation of KCN with trace amounts of water, quickly leads to shutdown of the catalytic activity.<citation rid="cit8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21699208" doi="10.1021/ja2042035" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="cit26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18336024" doi="10.1021/ja078298h" count="1">26</citation> <sentence_start/>Still this deactivation is a combined result of Pd(0) undergoing oxidative addition into the H-CN bond followed by trapping of this species with excess cyanide anion to generate off-cycle palladium(<sc>ii</sc>) cyanide complexes. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, there was not a clear indication why certain heteroaryl bromides were successful coupling partners with HCN, whereas others were not. <sentence_start/>With the exception of the protocol developed by Buchwald and Hooker, in which H<sup>11</sup>CN is used to form PET tracers, no reports are found on palladium-catalysed cyanation of aryl halides using gaseous HCN as the reactant.<citation rid="cit21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25565277" doi="10.1021/ja512115s" pmcid="PMC4394387" count="1">21</citation> <sentence_start/>Although it should be noted under the conditions used for <sup>11</sup>C-isotope-labelling, the Pd(<sc>ii</sc>)-aryl complex is in an approx. 1000-fold excess compared to the H<sup>11</sup>CN generated. <sentence_start/>With this in mind it was decided to take a closer look at the possible mechanism for the developed protocol.

The overall accepted mechanism for the Pd-catalysed cyanation using sodium or potassium cyanide is believed to go through an initial oxidative addition of the Pd(0) complex into the aryl halide, nucleophilic displacement by cyanide on the formed palladium(<sc>ii</sc>) centre, and lastly a reductive elimination furnishing the desired benzonitrile (Scheme 5).<citation rid="cit6h" ref-type="bibr" count="1">6h</citation>,<citation rid="cit7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21528150" doi="10.1039/c1cs15004a" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="cit8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21699208" doi="10.1021/ja2042035" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="cit26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18336024" doi="10.1021/ja078298h" count="1">26</citation> <sentence_start/>When metal complexes such as Zn(CN)<sub>2</sub> are utilised, a change in mechanism occurs, whereby nucleophilic substitution is replaced with a transmetallation step.<citation rid="cit9b" ref-type="bibr" count="1">9b</citation>,<citation rid="cit34" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18980375" doi="10.1021/ol8016935" count="1">34</citation>

<sentence_start/>After formation of the catalytically active palladium(0) species, two reversible oxidative addition events take place forming L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(H)(CN) and L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(Ar)(Br). <sentence_start/>The necessity for the oxidative addition steps to be reversible at least for the latter complex may explain why aryl triflates are not competent electrophiles for this catalytic protocol. <sentence_start/>The two complexes can then undergo transmetallation providing L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(Ar)(CN) and L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(H)(Br). <sentence_start/>Similar transmetallative events have previously been reported for two Pd(<sc>ii</sc>)-aryl species.<citation rid="cit43" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28399364" doi="10.1021/jacs.7b01970" pmcid="PMC5485668" count="1">43</citation> <sentence_start/>Finally, the benzonitrile and the active L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(0) species are reformed through two reductive elimination events involving both L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(Ar)(CN) and L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(H)(Br). <sentence_start/>In the latter case, base is required to initiate the regeneration of L<italic toggle="yes"><sub>n</sub></italic>Pd(0), and the presence of aqueous KOAc should be sufficient for promoting this reduction step at the metal centre. <sentence_start/>Whereas stronger bases would be able to carry out this step as well, they would also lead to Conclusions

In summary, a new protocol for the direct use of stoichiometric gaseous hydrogen cyanide in the Pd-catalysed cyanation of aryl bromides has been developed. <sentence_start/>Contrary to previous studies, the use of HCN did not lead to catalytic shutdown, but instead provided a robust and reproducible method. <sentence_start/>A broad range of aryl bromides and a few heteroaromatic bromides afforded the desired benzonitrile derivatives and given the simple setup, utilising <italic toggle="yes">ex situ</italic> generation of HCN, labelling with H<sup>13</sup>CN was also straightforward. <sentence_start/>The presence of water as co-solvent and the use of the mild base KOAc proved imperative for catalytic efficiency. <sentence_start/>In particular, the suitability of this weak base indicated that possibly the mechanism in operation deviates from previous catalytic cyanation studies as the concentration of free cyanide would be virtually non-existent. <sentence_start/>This led to the proposal of a mechanism based on a transmetallation between two Pd-complexes produced from the oxidative addition of Pd(0) into hydrogen cyanide and an aryl bromide. <sentence_start/>This proposal was based on mechanistic indications that co-aligns with observations reported by Grushin, Beller and others. <sentence_start/>Further work is now on-going to examine a similar protocol under nickel catalysis, as well as examining other electrophiles than aryl halides. <sentence_start/>The results of this work will be reported in due course.
